name: AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC)
description: A dataset consisting of 7,787 natural, grade-school science multiple-choice questions authored for standardized tests, partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set, along with the ARC Corpus of 14M science-related sentences and baseline models to encourage research in advanced question answering.
creator: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord
citeAs: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord. Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge.
rai:dataCollection: The ARC dataset was assembled through several months of extensive search and investigation to obtain publicly releasable natural science questions authored for standardized tests. The dataset consists of 7,787 non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions drawn from a variety of sources and partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set. The Challenge Set was operationally defined as questions answered incorrectly by both a retrieval-based solver and a PMI-based co-occurrence solver. In addition, the ARC Corpus was created by using a major search engine to run a large series of automatically constructed science-related queries based on about 100 hand-written templates for 80 science topics; top documents were collected, deduplicated, stripped to text, and chunked into sentences, then augmented with the AristoMini corpus.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources for the question set were standardized test science questions from a variety of sources, including state assessment programs and an anonymous content partner ('Mercury'). The ARC Corpus raw data came from Web documents retrieved via a major search engine using science-topic query templates, plus the AristoMini corpus containing Wiktionary definitions, Simple Wikipedia science articles, and additional science sentences collected from the Web.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were sorted into a Challenge Set of 2,590 questions and an Easy Set of 5,197 questions based on whether both the IR solver and PMI solver failed to answer them correctly. For the ARC Corpus, retrieved documents were de-duplicated, stripped down to text, chunked into sentences, and augmented with AristoMini.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the ARC Corpus, the top several documents from each search were collected and de-duplicated, document content was stripped down to capture just the text, and the resulting text was chunked into sentences. For entailment-based baselines, retrieved sentences were filtered to require the answer choice, long sentences (>300 characters), sentences with negation, and noisy sentences were filtered, and the top 8 sentences were selected based on ElasticSearch score. For question-to-assertion conversion, questions were converted into fill-in-the-blank statements by replacing wh-words with a blank and dropping phrases common in multiple-choice settings such as 'of the following' and 'of these'.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset uses existing multiple-choice science questions authored for human standardized tests, with correct answers provided as part of those test questions. No new human annotation process for labeling the ARC questions is described. For analysis purposes, the authors enumerated broad classes of knowledge and reasoning types observed in the ARC Challenge based on a sample of 100 questions, noting that this required subjective judgment. The SciTail dataset mentioned for training entailment models was annotated by crowdworkers as entailing or not, but this is not annotation of ARC itself.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For the analysis of question types, the authors state that the relative sizes of knowledge and reasoning categories are necessarily approximate because identifying the main challenge exhibited by different questions requires subjective judgment.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The ARC Dataset, Corpus, Models, and Leaderboard can be accessed at http://data.allenai.org/arc. The paper notes that for up-to-date results users should see the ARC leaderboard, and that the dataset, corpus, three baseline neural models, and leaderboard are available from the ARC website.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Question grade level is included, ranging from 3rd grade to 9th grade, corresponding to students typically of age 8 through 13 years.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is presented to encourage AI research in advanced question answering and to move the field toward more difficult tasks requiring reasoning, commonsense knowledge, and deeper text comprehension rather than surface-level retrieval.
rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses that many prior QA datasets are biased toward surface-level cues and simple algorithms, and ARC was designed to reduce this by creating a Challenge partition. The authors also note retrieval bias in baseline systems: underlying IR methods favor sentences very similar to the question and disfavor sentences that only partially match individually but together explain the correct answer. They also note that progress on some datasets may be heavily concentrated on easy questions alone.
rai:dataLimitations: The operational definition of a Challenge question only approximates the informal goal of being a 'hard' question. The questions are difficult to obtain because examination boards release only limited practice tests publicly. The ARC Corpus contains indirect mentions of relevant knowledge, and exploiting them is not trivial. The paper also notes that identifying knowledge and reasoning categories is approximate and subjective. For question-to-assertion conversion, the simple fill-in-the-blank approach can produce non-grammatical sentences, and a more sophisticated rule-based approach was left to future work.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a challenge benchmark for advanced question answering research. It includes train/dev/test partitions for both the Challenge and Easy sets and is used for evaluating QA systems and baselines. The ARC Corpus is released as an optional supporting corpus; systems are not restricted to using it.
